text.title: Quit Day Job Trigger Contract Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules every quit-day-job trigger contract MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The trigger metric is net MRR as defined by the billing provider's MRR report (Stripe Billing, Baremetrics, ChartMogul or equivalent): recurring subscriptions only, annual and quarterly plans normalised to a monthly amount, discounts and refunds deducted, one-time fees, setup charges, trials and unpaid invoices excluded. The contract names the report and the provider; a spreadsheet the builder maintains by hand is not the metric.

rationale.source: Stripe Billing, Baremetrics and ChartMogul MRR definitions (vendor documentation)

rule.rationale: The number that feels like $4,000 is usually gross cash in a good month: three annual plans booked at once, a $500 onboarding fee, two trials that will not convert. Net MRR from the provider strips all of it and is the same number a buyer or an accountant would compute, which is the point of a contract you sign with your future self.

rule.statement: The trigger fires only after N consecutive month-end MRR readings at or above the threshold, with N at least 3. Readings are taken on the last day of each calendar month from the provider report; an intra-month peak, a partial month, or two qualifying months separated by a miss do not count, and the count restarts after any miss.

rationale.source: Widely established SaaS-metrics practice (month-end MRR snapshots); this methodology's valid example (3 consecutive months above)

rule.rationale: A launch week, a Product Hunt day or a pile of annual plans can push MRR over the line for one reading and back under it by the next. Three consecutive month-ends is the cheapest test that the number is a plateau and not a spike, and it is exactly the test a builder skips when the spike is exciting.

rule.statement: The trigger has a runway co-condition: liquid personal savings divided by monthly personal burn MUST be at least R months at the moment the MRR window completes, with R written in the contract (the valid example uses 12). Burn is taken from the runway model and includes income tax on self-employment, health insurance, and business costs; the contract prints the burn figure, the savings figure and the date they were computed.

rationale.source: side-project-financial-runway (sibling methodology); widely established personal-finance emergency-fund practice

rule.rationale: $4,000 MRR is not a $4,000 salary. After processor fees, tax at self-employed rates, health insurance and hosting, the take-home is materially lower, and the first bad quarter arrives before the tax bill does. Runway is what makes the bad quarter survivable; without it the MRR trigger is a ticket to a second, worse job search.

rule.statement: The reversal clause is numeric and dated: MRR below a reversal threshold for M consecutive month-ends, or runway below a reversal floor. The reversal MRR threshold MUST be strictly lower than the trigger threshold and the reversal window at least 2 months, so that trigger and reversal cannot both fire inside one quarter. A reversal clause with no number or no window is rejected.

rationale.source: Hysteresis as used in control engineering, applied to decision rules; this methodology's valid example (trigger 4000, reversal 3000)

rule.rationale: A trigger at $4,000 and a reversal at $4,000 flip-flops on noise: quit in March, panic in April, re-apply in May. The gap between the two numbers is the builder's tolerance for a bad month, decided in advance. The dated window is what stops "back to a job" being decided on the worst day of the worst month.

rule.statement: The contract states a maximum share of MRR from any single customer and a maximum monthly gross MRR churn, both as numbers (the builder sets them; a common shape is no customer above 20% and gross churn under 5% per month). The trigger does not fire while either gate is exceeded at any month-end in the window, even if MRR is above the threshold.

rationale.source: Widely established SaaS-metrics practice (customer concentration, gross MRR churn)

rule.rationale: $4,200 MRR made of one $3,000 customer and forty $30 customers is a consulting client with a login page. The day that customer leaves, the contract's trigger is still "fired" and the builder is unemployed with $1,200 MRR. The gates make the trigger measure a business, not a month.

rule.statement: The contract is committed as version 1.0.0, with a commit date, before the first month-end at which MRR reaches the threshold. Any later change to the threshold, N, R, the gates or the reversal clause bumps the version and records a one-line reason; changes made while a qualifying window is in progress are forbidden. A contract first committed after a qualifying reading is labelled `post_hoc: true` in its header.

rationale.source: Pre-commitment devices (Ulysses contracts) in behavioural economics; this methodology's purpose statement (decide before it is emotional)

rule.rationale: A contract written the week MRR crossed the line is a rationalisation with a schema. The whole instrument exists to bind the builder at the moment they are calm to the numbers they will want to bend at the moment they are not. The version bump plus reason makes the bending visible; the in-window freeze makes the most tempting bend impossible.

rule.statement: Every entry in `conclusion.evidence_links` resolves to the billing provider's MRR report or a dated export from it, or to the runway model file; each evidence item carries the month-end date it covers. A screenshot of a hand-maintained spreadsheet, a bank balance without the burn figure, or a link that does not resolve is rejected.

rationale.source: This methodology's output contract (evidence_links, format uri); anti-fabrication practice

rule.rationale: The builder is both the party and the auditor of this contract, which is the weakest possible control. A provider report with a date is the one input the builder cannot quietly edit at 23:00 in a bad month; a spreadsheet is.

rule.statement: The conclusion statement names the action, the date rule (for example "resign effective the first of the month after the third qualifying month-end"), the notice period, and who is informed and in what order. "Quit when ready" or a conclusion without a date rule is rejected.

rationale.source: This methodology's valid example and contract template (Conclusion: specific date or window)

rule.rationale: A trigger that fires into "I'll think about it" was never a trigger. The date rule turns a metric into a calendar event, and the notice period plus the order of conversations (partner, then manager, then customers) is what the builder will not be able to think through clearly on the day.

rule.statement: Each review at the contract's cadence (monthly or quarterly) appends the month-end MRR readings since the last review, the current runway in months, the concentration and churn gate values, and a verdict: `not_fired`, `window_in_progress` (with the count), `fired`, or `reversal_triggered`. A review entry without the numbers is not a review, and `review.last_run_at` is not updated by it.
rule.rationale: "Reviewed, still on track" written four quarters in a row is how a contract becomes folklore. The numbers in the review entry are the audit trail that shows whether the window is actually progressing, and they are what the builder reads on the emotional day to see how they got here.
